title: Checkpoint: Insects and Other Invertebrates
objective: After this level you can compare insects, spiders, mollusks and crustaceans.
summary: Insects, spiders and crustaceans are arthropods, with jointed legs and outer skeletons: about 84% of described animal species. Snails and earthworms are built another way.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: one word links the bee, the spider and the crab.
cards.body: They look nothing alike. Yet all three share a family name that means “jointed feet.” The snail and the earthworm don’t make the cut. Let’s line them up and see why.

cards.headline: Jointed feet, and a crowd
cards.body: All three are arthropods: animals with a jointed outer skeleton made of chitin bound to protein, and a segmented body whose segments carry jointed legs. The name says it: arthropod means “jointed feet.” By Britannica’s count, about 84 percent of described animal species are arthropods, most of them insects. If you picked an animal species at random, you’d very likely land on one.

cards.headline: Two outsiders without joints
cards.body: A snail has no jointed legs at all. It’s a mollusk: a soft body, often inside a shell its mantle makes, carried on one muscular foot. The earthworm has no jointed legs either: it’s a chain of ringlike segments that breathes through its skin. Same kingdom, same missing backbone, very different ways to build a body without one.

mascot.line: Joints, shells, slime or segments: the backbone-free crowd has tried every design.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: Insects: 3 parts, 6 legs; spiders: 2 parts, 8 legs
Crustaceans: calcium-stiffened shells, 2 pairs of antennae
All three are arthropods, about 84% of described species
Snails are mollusks on one muscular foot
Butterflies and mosquitoes: egg, larva, pupa, adult

questions.prompt: Insects and Other Invertebrates recap: what does the name “arthropod” mean?

options.label: Many legs
options.rationale: Close, but the name is about joints.

options.label: Hard shell
options.rationale: The shell isn’t in the name.

options.label: Six sides
options.rationale: That’s a honeycomb cell, not an arthropod.

questions.explanation: Arthropod means jointed feet: their segments bear jointed legs.

questions.prompt: Insects and Other Invertebrates recap: why isn’t a garden snail an arthropod?

options.label: It has a shell
options.rationale: Crabs have shells and are still arthropods.

options.label: It has no jointed legs; it moves on one muscular foot
It lives on land
options.rationale: Many arthropods, like insects and spiders, live on land.

options.label: It has a backbone
options.rationale: Snails are invertebrates, with no backbone.

questions.explanation: Arthropods have jointed legs; a snail is a mollusk that glides on a single muscular foot.

questions.prompt: Insects and Other Invertebrates recap: an animal has a shell stiffened with calcium carbonate and two pairs of antennae. What is it?

options.label: A honeybee
options.rationale: Insects have one pair of antennae.

options.label: A garden snail
options.rationale: Snails aren’t arthropods and have no such antennae.

questions.explanation: Two pairs of antennae and a calcium-stiffened exoskeleton mark a crustacean, like a lobster.

questions.prompt: Insects and Other Invertebrates recap, from Level 51: which part of an insect carries its legs and wings?

options.label: The head
options.rationale: The head carries eyes, mouthparts and antennae.

options.label: The abdomen
options.rationale: The abdomen holds the digestive and reproductive organs.

options.label: The antennae
options.rationale: Antennae are on the head and carry nothing.

questions.explanation: The thorax, the middle part, carries an insect’s six legs and, in most adults, its wings.

questions.prompt: Insects and Other Invertebrates recap: which two animals from this chapter both pass through egg, larva, pupa and adult?

options.label: Garden snail and earthworm
options.rationale: Neither was shown with a pupa stage.

options.label: Lobster and orb weaver
options.rationale: Neither has a pupa stage in this chapter.

questions.explanation: Monarchs and Anopheles mosquitoes both go through egg, larva, pupa and adult: complete metamorphosis.
